Title: Laying the Foundation for Economic Success, Brick by Brick
Chunks: 0,1
Frank Cordie grew up across the river from St. Louis, MO in Belleville, IL. After college, he took his first job at a refractory plant in Mexico, MO – the Fire Brick Capital of the World, and home to a leading refractory manufacturing company, A.P. Green Refractories. Frank spent the next 25 years working in the brick-manufacturing industry, managing several plants for multiple companies. Frank eventually returned to Mexico, MO as the Vice President of Manufacturing for A.P. Green. By the late 1990s, A.P. Green had been purchased by another company, and the refractory industry in the U.S. had consolidated to just a few manufacturers. Frank’s position meant he was responsible for, among other things, consolidating production and closing plants where necessary. The A.P. Green factory, a cornerstone of the Mexico community, was shuttered in 2002.
Mid America Brick CEO Frank Cordie at the company's plant in Mexico, MO, July 6, 2011. (Photo by Employees of Mid America Brick)
In December 2006, Frank began a process to bring brick manufacturing back to Mexico, MO. His goal was to purchase and re-purpose the former A.P. Green plant to produce face brick used in residential and commercial construction. Engaging in what would be eventually described as “one of the most complicated financing projects in the United States” by partner Advantage Capital, the intricacies of the deal took almost four years to complete. Frank leveraged local, State, and Federal New Market Tax Credits, loans and loan guarantee programs – including a Rural Business and Industry Loan Guarantee from the USDA. An initial investment of $500,000 from an LLC formed by local businessmen – described by Frank as “the snowball at the top of the mountain” – eventually became a total startup investment of almost $22 million.
In addition to Advantage Capital, supporters in the venture included companies from Buffalo, NY, St. Louis, MO, and Knoxville, TN. A bipartisan group of city, state, and federal elected officials and legislators worked together to make the project a reality.

On June 25, 2010, Mid America Brick was unveiled with 400 community members in attendance 100 years after the founding of A.P. Green at the same location. The community has rallied around the project. Local accountants and lawyers provided services free of charge during the financing process, telling Frank they knew he’d reimburse them when the venture succeeded. A retired businessman and initial investor personally mowed the lawn, cleaned the parking lot, and provided a new flagpole for the facility in advance of the unveiling. Frank’s wife Judy worked to revive the Mexico community Christmas Tree lighting – a long standing tradition of the A.P. Green Company – last December. Retired A.P. Green employees volunteered time, expertise, and materials so Mid America Brick could hold an event for which they didn’t plan a budget. At the tree lighting, Judy and Frank collected donations for The Help Center, a local food pantry and clothing supplier for those in need.
Mid America Brick extruded its first brick on April 13, 2011. The company is now the only brick manufacturer in central Missouri. They have 42 full-time employees, and hope to expand to 75 employees by the end of next year, by which time they expect to produce over 60 million bricks annually. They have also supported related areas of labor, contracting out clay mining in the surrounding area, hauling and trucking 10-20 loads of clay and brick per day, and bringing in contractors for large maintenance projects. During the retrofitting of the facility, 50-75 workers assisted on construction, helping the hotel and restaurant industries in Mexico, MO. The company has also been recognized by the State of Missouri for its efforts employing veterans.
Mid America Brick is helping to lead a revitalization of Mexico, MO. Mid America Brick provides an independent, local source of bricks for residential and commercial construction in Missouri and surrounding states. The company’s goal is “to be the preferred brick supplier for all customers, by providing quality products and superior service.”
_Ari Matusiak is Executive Director of the White House Business Council_

Title: ‘Firebrick Capital’ looks to face brick for jobs
Chunks: 0,1,2
Updated June 5, 2010, 7:00 a.m. CT
Mexico, Mo., once again will be the home to a brick-making facility, but this time it will produce bricks for the homebuilding market and not to line furnaces.
Once known as the “Firebrick Capital of the World” for its abundance of manufacturers of bricks used to line industrial furnaces, Mexico saw its economic fortunes dwindle as the brick facilities closed one by one.
End of an era for Cleek’sTop 10 CEO Undergraduate Alma MatersKampai Sushi Bar & Restaurant
Midway USA
The A.P. Green firebrick plant, which had been in operation since 1910, closed in 2001. At its height during World War II, the plant employed nearly 4,000 workers. At the end it had 118 on its payroll. The following year, 2002, Mexico’s last brick factory closed, taking with it 200 jobs.
This week, on the 100th anniversary of the opening of the A.P. Green factory, Mid America Brick & Structural Clay Products LLC closed on the purchase of 100 acres and the buildings on the former A.P. Green site.
The cost of the purchase and for recommissioning the 500,000-square-foot former A.P. Green facility is $21.9 million.
Mexico became the so-called “Firebrick Capital of the World” because the region’s clay was so heat-resistant and conducive to making firebricks, which are used in industrial furnaces. Mexico icon A.P. Green, maternal grandfather of U.S. Sen. Kit Bond, wrote that he thought “the quality of Missouri clays, if properly exploited, would result in establishing Missouri as the leading fire brick business in the United States and later of the world.”
However, with the decline in the industries that use such furnaces — steel, cement and others — the demand has declined. Mid America Brick will manufacture so-called face brick, which is used for residential and commercial construction.
CEO Frank Cordie said in a statement that when fully operational, the company will create as many as 80 new jobs and produce more than 60 million bricks per year. Vice President David Adams said the company hopes to begin producing bricks by next spring.

Adams said they’re confident in the market because homebuilding is picking up and face brick inventories are at all-time lows. He said the closest face brick plant is in Jackson in southeast Missouri.
“It’s great news for us,” Adams said of the building turnaround, “in addition to brick inventories are at the lowest level they’ve been in some time. We look forward to capitalizing on that.”
The deal for the A.P. Green property, which has been in the works for four years, included local, state and federal grants and loans.
St. Louis-based Advantage Capital Partners provided $9.75 million for the project.
NO NEEEED FOR A BUILDING
The former Cleek’s store at Worley Street and West Boulevard has been demolished, and property owner and local rent-to-own king “Tiger” John Cleek said he’s looking at a couple of different options for the property.
Cleek estimates the building is about 60 years old. He moved out his business about 18 months ago when he joined Aaron Rents Inc. and set up shop at the Aaron’s store on Business Loop 70 West.
The building had been remodeled in 2004, but Cleek says it “just needed more work done to it than was reasonable to do to it.”
Cleek said the building was home to Bob’s Market when he was a child. and his father bought it in 1971. Cleek moved in in August 1973.
SUNDAY NEWS
KMIZ-TV is introducing a 30-minute community affairs show called “ABC 17 News This Week.” The first episode is scheduled for 11 a.m. tomorrow. The show will be hosted by anchor Ryan Tate and feature in-depth exploration of community issues, said ABC 17 News Director Curtis Varns. Tomorrow’s broadcast will be a look at the state budget.
Varns said he has been at the station for more than 15 years and during that time they’ve added about nine hours of news to each broadcast week, but this is the first regularly scheduled 30-minute newsmagazine the station has done.

“Money has been so tight on the federal, state and local levels the past few years that people are looking for accountability in their elected officials more than ever,” Varns said. “We try to take a critical look at the issues every time we cover state and local government in our nightly news. We should be able to build on that effort in this format.”
QUICKIES
**The University of Missouri** made an appearance on BusinessWeek.com’s Top 10 CEO Undergraduate Alma Maters list. MU tied with Harvard, the University of Texas and the University of Wisconsin with 11 CEOs. David Novak of Yum! Brands was highlighted on the list for MU. … Internet shooting retailer **Midway USA** has branched out into archery gear. The company that bills itself as offering “Just About Everything for Shooting, Reloading, Gunsmithing and Hunting” has now begun offering arrows and arrow shafts; broadheads and points; archery sights; shooting releases; quivers; archery targets; bow cases; and bow tuning products. … **Kampai Sushi Bar & Restaurant,** 907 Alley A, is now open. The restaurant, owned by Art Wuttisak, Tony Sudsai and Sam Tuankrua, is near Ninth Street, just south of Broadway.

Updated June 5, 2010, 7:00 a.m. CT
Mexico, Mo., once again will be the home to a brick-making facility, but this time it will produce bricks for the homebuilding market and not to line furnaces.
Once known as the “Firebrick Capital of the World” for its abundance of manufacturers of bricks used to line industrial furnaces, Mexico saw its economic fortunes dwindle as the brick facilities closed one by one.
End of an era for Cleek’sTop 10 CEO Undergraduate Alma MatersKampai Sushi Bar & Restaurant

The A.P. Green firebrick plant, which had been in operation since 1910, closed in 2001. At its height during World War II, the plant employed nearly 4,000 workers. At the end it had 118 on its payroll. The following year, 2002, Mexico’s last brick factory closed, taking with it 200 jobs.
This week, on the 100th anniversary of the opening of the A.P. Green factory, Mid America Brick & Structural Clay Products LLC closed on the purchase of 100 acres and the buildings on the former A.P. Green site.
The cost of the purchase and for recommissioning the 500,000-square-foot former A.P. Green facility is $21.9 million.
Mexico became the so-called “Firebrick Capital of the World” because the region’s clay was so heat-resistant and conducive to making firebricks, which are used in industrial furnaces. Mexico icon A.P. Green, maternal grandfather of U.S. Sen. Kit Bond, wrote that he thought “the quality of Missouri clays, if properly exploited, would result in establishing Missouri as the leading fire brick business in the United States and later of the world.”
However, with the decline in the industries that use such furnaces — steel, cement and others — the demand has declined. Mid America Brick will manufacture so-called face brick, which is used for residential and commercial construction.
CEO Frank Cordie said in a statement that when fully operational, the company will create as many as 80 new jobs and produce more than 60 million bricks per year. Vice President David Adams said the company hopes to begin producing bricks by next spring.
texts.1:
Adams said they’re confident in the market because homebuilding is picking up and face brick inventories are at all-time lows. He said the closest face brick plant is in Jackson in southeast Missouri.
“It’s great news for us,” Adams said of the building turnaround, “in addition to brick inventories are at the lowest level they’ve been in some time. We look forward to capitalizing on that.”
The deal for the A.P. Green property, which has been in the works for four years, included local, state and federal grants and loans.
St. Louis-based Advantage Capital Partners provided $9.75 million for the project.
NO NEEEED FOR A BUILDING
The former Cleek’s store at Worley Street and West Boulevard has been demolished, and property owner and local rent-to-own king “Tiger” John Cleek said he’s looking at a couple of different options for the property.
Cleek estimates the building is about 60 years old. He moved out his business about 18 months ago when he joined Aaron Rents Inc. and set up shop at the Aaron’s store on Business Loop 70 West.
The building had been remodeled in 2004, but Cleek says it “just needed more work done to it than was reasonable to do to it.”
Cleek said the building was home to Bob’s Market when he was a child. and his father bought it in 1971. Cleek moved in in August 1973.
SUNDAY NEWS
KMIZ-TV is introducing a 30-minute community affairs show called “ABC 17 News This Week.” The first episode is scheduled for 11 a.m. tomorrow. The show will be hosted by anchor Ryan Tate and feature in-depth exploration of community issues, said ABC 17 News Director Curtis Varns. Tomorrow’s broadcast will be a look at the state budget.
Varns said he has been at the station for more than 15 years and during that time they’ve added about nine hours of news to each broadcast week, but this is the first regularly scheduled 30-minute newsmagazine the station has done.
texts.2:
